name: Asylum -- Refugee Status Determination (UNHCR-Administered)

qualifying_event.description: A person with a well-founded fear of persecution may register with UNHCR Jordan, which conducts refugee status determination (RSD) directly under a Memorandum of Understanding with the Jordanian government -- Jordan is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol and has no domestic asylum law.
qualifying_event.evidence_hint: Registration with UNHCR; identity documents where available.

requirements.blocker_text: Registration with UNHCR Jordan, which issues an asylum-seeker certificate granting access to services and protection against refoulement pending a decision.
Well-founded fear of persecution meeting the international refugee definition, assessed by UNHCR's RSD unit against international refugee law (Jordan has no domestic refugee law of its own to apply).

outcome.duration_length: asylum-seeker certificate pending RSD; if recognised, refugee certificate -- fixed post-recognition duration not confirmed in this pass

sources.title: UNHCR Jordan -- Refugee Status Determination: UNHCR itself runs RSD in Jordan (not a domestic government agency), issues asylum-seeker and refugee certificates, feedback on inquiries within ~3 weeks, appeal window of 1 month via SMS after a decision

notes: NEW COUNTRY BUILD (Jordan). STATUS: DRAFT -- STRUCTURALLY DISTINCT from most countries in this dataset: Jordan hosts one of the largest refugee populations in the world (chiefly Syrian, alongside long-standing Iraqi and Palestinian populations) but is NOT a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or 1967 Protocol and has no domestic asylum law -- refugee status determination is conducted directly by UNHCR under a Memorandum of Understanding with the government (first signed 1998, subsequently amended), not by a Jordanian ministry. This is a different shape of 'absence' than Vietnam's or Oman's total absence of any protection mechanism (see those countries' files): Jordan has a large, functioning, internationally-run protection system, just not a domestic legal one -- disclosed explicitly rather than modeled as either a full domestic system or a total absence. Work rights are heavily conditioned in practice (the well-documented Syrian refugee work-permit scheme is a partial, sector-limited exception administered by the Ministry of Labour, not modeled as its own file here since it is an employment accommodation for a specific existing refugee population rather than a general immigration route). Post-recognition status duration and family reunification mechanics were not confirmed in this pass -- family_can_join is set true as a conservative default consistent with UNHCR's general global family-reunification practice for recognised refugees, not a Jordan-specific confirmation; family_can_work is set false since the source only referenced work permits for a specific existing refugee population (Syrians) rather than a general dependent work right.
